Citi downgraded tech to neutral and expects defensives to keep beating economically sensitive sectors into next year. Since the Nasdaq 100 peaked on October 6, P&G is up about 10%. I couldn't find what drove today's 7.5% drop. I found no Arrowhead news release, no broker downgrade and no news story dated Nov 13–16, so it looks like the selling simply continued without a new headline. I ran out of web searches before I could check whether Ionis or the biotech sector fell today, so that is still open; I can pick it up in a follow-up.

## The story

**The business.** Arrowhead makes RNAi drugs, which switch off a disease-causing gene in the liver and need only infrequent shots. It now has one product on the market: Redemplo (plozasiran), approved for FCS, a very rare inherited disorder that drives triglycerides (a blood fat) extremely high. Approvals cover the US, EU, UK, Canada, China and Australia, and Sanofi holds the rights in Greater China. The big prize is sHTG, a much more common form of very high triglycerides, which management sizes at **$3–4 billion a year** in the US. In its two Phase 3 trials, Redemplo cut triglycerides 79–81% and episodes of acute pancreatitis 78%, with results published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

**Why the stock broke (Nov 9).** Ionis sells Tryngolza, the rival drug, which is already approved for sHTG and dosed monthly; Redemplo is dosed every three months. On Nov 9 Ionis cut its 2026 Tryngolza sales forecast to about **$50M from $100–110M**, blaming a "more gradual launch ramp" as doctors slowly adopt a new way of treating the condition. It also cut its net price, and commercial insurance covered only 33% of patients at the end of September. Ionis stock fell about 27%. Arrowhead fell 15–19% the same day, from about $58.2 to about $47–49, on roughly twice its normal volume. The market read Tryngolza's slow start as a warning that the whole sHTG market will build slowly, which is exactly the market Arrowhead's valuation depends on. Ionis now also faces law-firm notices of a possible securities investigation.

**Earnings (Nov 12).** Results were weak, and the stock fell about 4.5% to $47.15.
- **Revenue:** $450.8M for the year to Sept 30, down 46% because last year included one-off licensing payments from Sarepta and Sanofi. Fourth-quarter revenue was $37.8M against about $62.6M expected.
- **Loss:** $724M, or $5.11 a share. That includes $215M spent buying a priority review voucher, a transferable credit that shortens an FDA review.
- **Redemplo sales:** only about $6.6M in its first year.
- **Prescriptions:** new prescriptions rose 63% quarter on quarter to 950, then passed 1,250 by early November, now running at about 50–60 a week. Prescribers grew from 640 to more than 860, and insurance covers about 160M US lives.
- **Bright spots:**
  - **Faster FDA review:** The sHTG application went in on Nov 2 and was accepted into an FDA pilot program with a six-month review and a chance of an earlier decision. That suggests a decision around **May 2027 or sooner**, with a US launch targeted for Q2 2027. The company did not give an exact decision date.
  - **Voucher kept:** Because of the pilot, Arrowhead didn't need its voucher and still holds it.
  - **Cheaper debt:** The company swapped a 15% loan for a $400M loan at SOFR plus 5.5%, maturing in 2031.
  - **Cash:** $1.19B, against $683M of convertible notes and a $400M liability from selling future royalties.

**Analysts.**
- Stifel cut its target to $96 from $104 and kept Buy, citing the Tryngolza read-through.
- RBC kept Outperform with a $100 target on Nov 13.
- Goldman is Neutral at $74, the lowest target.
- Wall Street Zen, a ratings site rather than a brokerage, cut the stock to Strong Sell on Nov 14.
- The consensus target is about $99, so most analysts still hold Buy-type ratings and haven't capitulated.

**Other programs, all early:**
- **Obesity:** ARO-INHBE and ARO-ALK7, with small Phase 1/2a data sets. The one weight-loss readout was four patients on Lilly's tirzepatide losing 9.4% versus 4.8% for those on placebo.
- **Alzheimer's:** ARO-MAPT cut tau protein in spinal fluid by up to 73% in October.
- **HoFH:** Zodasiran's Phase 3, for an inherited form of very high cholesterol, reads out in mid-2027.

## What it means for a 1–10 session trade

**Next known event:** a fireside chat at the Jefferies London healthcare conference on **Wed Nov 18**. That is the first chance for management to talk about launch pace since earnings. There are no other dated catalysts before the FDA decision in 2027.

**Case for a bounce:**
- The stock is down roughly 54% from its $95 high and very oversold.
- Its drug won both Phase 3 trials outright, and the FDA review is on a fast track.
- Cash is about $1.2B.
- No new bad news came out today.

**Case against:**
- Nothing on the calendar can change the main worry, a slow sHTG launch, until 2027.
- Nearly every recent data point was bad: Ionis's guidance cut, a revenue miss, small sales and more broker target cuts.
- Today's drop came with no headline on normal volume, which looks like steady selling rather than a washout.
- The stock is about $7 above its 52-week low of $37.06.
- If the Jefferies remarks repeat what was said at earnings, they won't help.

  - From October 13 to November 11 it gained 18.6% while the S&P lost 2.3%. The dividend yields about 5.8%.
  - Risks:
    - The pricing and mix gains fade as the Amazon cuts are lapped.
    - Volume comparisons stay negative through the first half of 2027.
    - The Q4 U.S. margin target of about 10.5% is the number to watch.
    - Next earnings are in January.
- **FDX (parcel), the self-help name.**
  - On October 28, its first report on the new calendar fiscal year, adjusted EPS was $3.74 against $3.36 expected. 2026 EPS guidance rose to $18.00–18.60. FedEx Freight was spun off in June and now trades as FDXF.

  - Small negatives: the interim CFO sold about $5.3M of stock on November 10, and a new CFO (Jamere Jackson) starts November 30.
- **EXPD (freight forwarder), riding AI shipments.**
  - Q3 on November 3: revenue up 42% to $4.1B, EPS up 62% to $2.65 (about $0.42 above consensus). Air tonnage rose 13% (19% in September) on demand from the big AI data-center builders, and ocean volume rose 12%.

  - It beat Q3 on October 28 (adjusted EPS $1.80) but fell about 10%. The drags were the $5.8B RXO purchase announced October 5, cost inflation, and a unanimous May 2026 Supreme Court ruling that lets brokers be sued over the carriers they pick. That case was against CH Robinson.

- **A broad tech sell-off.** The S&P 500 fell about 1.9% and the Nasdaq about 2.5%. Chip stocks were hit by tighter export rules and nerves before Nvidia's earnings, and the VIX (the volatility index) reached about 23–24.

- **Insurers have played safe haven before.** On July 28, 2026, the S&P 500 insurance index closed at a record while the Nasdaq slid on AI worries (Bloomberg). Today repeats that pattern. The ten names have little to do with AI or chips, and higher rates help them.

**Rates help these companies, for now**
- The 10-year Treasury yield is around 5.1% (it touched 5.31% on October 5). The Fed raised rates in September, and Kalshi traders put about 79% odds on another hike on December 9.
- Insurers invest their float (premiums held until claims are paid) mostly in bonds, so higher yields lift their income. Chubb earns about 6.2% on new money against a 5.2% portfolio yield and had record investment income in the third quarter. Travelers and Cincinnati Financial also reported investment income up 7–10%.
- The catch is that higher yields cut the value of bonds they already hold. Chubb took $4.5 billion of realized and unrealized losses, and Allstate had $545 million of investment losses.

- **Commercial pricing is near flat.**
  - Travelers' renewal rate increase was 0.9%, down from 4.3% a year ago, and US commercial property premiums fell about 4%.
  - Chubb says competition is growing "across the board." Its North American commercial combined ratio worsened to 86.3 from 81.5. (Combined ratio is claims plus expenses per $100 of premium, so lower is better.)

- **Reinsurance is weaker still.** Property-catastrophe reinsurance rates are expected to fall another 10% or more at the January 1 renewals (KBW, Fitch, Moody's). Arch's reinsurance premiums fell 8–9%, and its CEO called casualty margins "zero or turning negative."

  |---|---|---|

  | Chubb | $705M | $285M |

- **CB:** strong investment income, softening commercial pricing.
- **TRV:** a big earnings beat, but rate increases are near zero.

That includes current positioning. Also, the search budget ran out before I could look for the bearish case, so the risks below come only from the sources I'd already read.

## The story

The dollar is in a rally driven by expected Fed rate hikes, and it has reached a 19-month high.

- **Where it stands:** The Dollar Index is about 103.5 to 103.66, its highest since April 2, 2025, the day the tariffs were announced. Its 52-week low was 95.55 on January 27, 2026, so it is up about 8% since then. Six straight up days this week followed five up days last week.
- **How it got here:** Gains began early in 2026 when the Fed stopped cutting rates. They sped up in late August after Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech and the hikes that followed.
- **This leg's trigger:** October CPI, released on November 10, came in hot: headline +0.4% against +0.3% expected, core +0.3%. Fed officials then pushed:
  - Waller said he would consider a 0.5-point hike in December.
  - Logan said "at least two more" 0.25-point hikes are needed.
  - Goolsbee called the CPI "borderline disturbing."
- **Fed pricing:**
  - A December hike is treated as certain (CME FedWatch about 100%).
  - Odds of a 0.5-point hike fell to about 4%.
  - About 0.43 points of hikes are priced by January, so markets also expect a follow-up hike early in 2027.
  - The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.1%.
- **Monday's session:**
  - The Nasdaq fell 2.5%, semiconductors fell 5.4%, and Nvidia hit its lowest since July 2025.
  - AI sentiment is shaken by the CEO's sudden departure and doubts over debt-funded AI spending.
  - Oil fell 3.3% to $84.38.
  - The dollar still rose about 0.2% to a new high. Hike expectations and some safe-haven buying outweighed falling oil and slightly lower yields (10-year down about 4bp).
  - Warsh's speech at about 11:09 AM CT covered AI and productivity, with no signal on rates.
- **The other currencies:** The euro is about 58% of the index. It is at a 19-month low near $1.0985, and the ECB has no meeting this week. The yen is about 14% and sits near 159.5 to 160 per dollar.

## What could move it in the next 1–10 sessions

- **Tuesday 11/17, retail sales at 7:30 AM CT:** The consensus is about flat to +0.2% headline and +0.4% excluding autos. Sources say a weak print could ease hike bets and hurt the dollar.
- **Tuesday after the close:** Nvidia earnings, its first since the CEO left. A bad result could set off another AI selloff. Whether that lifts or hurts the dollar is unclear (see the third risk below).
- **Wednesday 11/18:** October FOMC minutes. Signs of urgency would raise the odds of a 0.5-point hike.
- **Friday 11/20:** Japan's October CPI and final University of Michigan sentiment.
- **BoJ:** It has about a 75% chance of a December hike.

## Risks to the trend

1. **Japan intervening near 160 yen per dollar.** Japan's top currency official, Mimura, called recent moves "too fast" and pointed to the summer intervention. Buying yen would knock the index down directly, and that is the most likely trigger for a sharp one-day drop.
2. **Falling oil and tighter financial conditions.** MUFG names these as what it would take to push back on hike expectations, and oil is already falling. Stocks falling and yields above 5% are a tightening.
3. **AI-equity correction.** CBA's Kong is bullish on the dollar because of AI-related money flowing into the US. She names "erratic US policymaking and a sharp correction in AI-related equities" as the key risks to that view. This is the tension: a selloff can lift the dollar as a haven, as it did on Monday, or hurt it by reversing those inflows.
4. **Crowding.** The latest positioning data I could find, from late September (StoneX), showed net-long dollar bets at a multi-year high. November data wasn't found. If that is still the case, a soft data print could trigger a sharp pullback.
5. **Fiscal worries.** Around the Democratic sweep in the midterms earlier this month, the dollar fell briefly as markets reassessed the fiscal outlook. It is a minor factor now.

## On the trend continuing

MUFG expects back-to-back 0.25-point hikes in December and January, which it says "should support the dollar into year-end." It sees limited room for the dollar to rise much past 160 yen but says the broader trend is hard to reverse. Strength against the euro, pound, Australian dollar and Swiss franc points the same way. Nothing I found says the trend has broken. The near-term questions are the risks above: whether Tuesday's retail sales and Nvidia results revive it or start a pause from a stretched level.

## The story in one line
For most of 2026 Edwards was a "TAVR is maturing" stock that sat in the $75–90 range. TAVR is its main product, a heart valve replaced through a catheter instead of open surgery. Over about two weeks in early November, three things turned the story into "TAVR is growing again, with new patient groups opening up":
- a trial result on Nov 2
- a better-than-expected quarter and a raised outlook on Nov 4
- a wave of analyst target raises on Nov 5

The stock hasn't had a meaningful pullback since. Holding flat today on a –1.9% SPY day was a show of relative strength, not a sign the run has stopped.

## Why it was depressed before
- **Growth worries:** through spring 2026 analysts worried about slowing TAVR growth and cut forecasts. Around late March the stock was near $79, and the 52-week low is $74.66.
- **Lost acquisition:** Edwards dropped its JenaValve deal after the FTC (the US competition regulator) won a court injunction. The stock fell 3.4% to about $79.
- **Downgrade:** Oppenheimer downgraded the stock ahead of trial readouts. Patent fights also weighed.
- **Flat stretch:** Trefis notes the stock was roughly flat over the ~57 sessions before the recent run. It traded near $88 going into the late-October heart conference.

## What changed
1. **PROGRESS trial (Nov 2), presented at the TCT heart conference and published in NEJM.** It tested TAVR in patients with *moderate* aortic narrowing who had risk features, against watchful waiting.
   - Death or heart-failure events at two years: 16.7% with TAVR vs 23.9% with waiting, a one-third reduction.
   - Heart-failure hospital stays: 7.4% vs 14.9%, which drove most of the benefit.
   - No difference in death rates.
   - Management says moderate patients outnumber severe ones about 2:1, so this could roughly double the pool of potential patients over time.
   - **Caveats:** Edwards funded the trial. The NEJM editorial called the patients "atypical" and said TAVR is not right for most moderate patients. The use still needs FDA approval, with timing to be given at the investor day.
2. **Q3 results (Nov 4).**
   - Sales: $1.72B, up 11.2% at constant currency, against $1.68B expected.
   - Adjusted EPS: $0.80, up 19%, against $0.74 expected.
   - TAVR: up 8.8%. Mitral and tricuspid valve sales: up 45.6%, to $207M.
   - Raised guidance: full-year sales growth to about 11.5% (from 10–11%), TAVR to 9–9.5% (from 8–9%), and EPS to $2.97–3.05.
   - Medicare's final coverage decision now covers patients with severe disease but no symptoms. Management expects a gradual effect through 2027, not a jump.
   - A $220M write-down cut GAAP EPS to $0.53 but did not matter to the market.
3. **Analyst raises (Nov 5 onward).**

   | Firm | Rating | Target |

   | Mizuho | — | $120 |

- **Valuation:** about 60 times trailing earnings, or about 35 times this year's expected EPS of roughly $3.01. Trefis calls the rally hard to justify, and InvestingPro rates the stock overvalued.

- **Medtronic:** reports conflict. Medtronic's long-term low-risk data showed more repeat procedures, which may help Edwards. But its SMART trial showed its Evolut valve doing better than Edwards' SAPIEN on valve dysfunction.

- **Nov 12 (Thu), the main catalyst:**

  - Raymond James: Market Perform, but notes early partner enthusiasm.

- **Consensus:** Hold, average target about 249.6 (8 Buy, 21 Hold, 4 Sell).
- **Valuation:** market cap about $10.6B at 217, trailing P/E about 52. Institutions own about 90%.

  - The catalysts are clean and recent: the founder's return plus a costly personal purchase.

## The story in one line
Wall Street is pricing **political risk, not weaker businesses**. On November 3 Democrats won both the House and the Senate. Elizabeth Warren is now in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and the 10% cap on credit card interest rates is back. The lenders' own third-quarter results and credit were good, and so were their remarks at a conference on November 11.

## Timeline of the twenty-session window (about Oct 19 to Nov 16)
- **Oct 20, SYF (Synchrony) Q3:** earnings beat ($2.68 a share against $2.42 expected). Net charge-offs, the loans written off as lost, fell to 4.79% from 5.16% a year earlier. Loans 30+ days late fell to 4.34%. Purchase volume rose 8%. It bought back $1.1B of stock in the quarter and has $4.6B left. **Shares still slipped.** Losses on the Walmart card are expected to build through 2027.
- **About Oct 21, COF (Capital One) Q3:** big beat, adjusted earnings of $6.69 a share against $5.50 expected. The charge-off rate fell to 2.73% from 3.23% the quarter before, helped by a $225M release of loan reserves. Cost savings from the Discover purchase are running about $1.8B a year. Shares rose only about 2.5–4%, with doubts about marketing spend (up 14%).
- **AXP (American Express):** Q3 earnings of $4.68 a share beat $4.51. Write-offs were 1.8%, and it raised its 2026 earnings forecast to $17.60–17.90 a share. It is also cutting about 5% of staff. The stock is down about 13% this year: $319.05 at today's close, with a 52-week range of $291–387.
- **Nov 3:** Democrats won both chambers, about 54 Senate seats and 228+ House seats.
- **Nov 4:** AmEx's CEO sold about $99M of stock from exercised options. COF's CEO also sold under a pre-set selling plan.

- **Nov 9–10:** Warren backed a 10% cap on CBS, and Senate Democrats formally revived it. She says she will work with Trump, who proposed the same cap in January. That makes it the rare bipartisan item. Republicans resisted it in January.
- **Nov 11, conference:** COF said credit is "strong," late payments are stable and capital is above 13% against the 11% it needs. It is blocking AI shopping agents from its system for now. A Wall Street bank note estimated that a 36% cap would cut earnings per share only about 2–3% at COF, SYF, Bread Financial and AXP. It said caps of 10–18% would mean "significant pressure."
- **Nov 16, today:** S&P down 1.92%, VIX (the volatility index) up 19% to 22.9. Selling was led by Nvidia and spread to banks, partly through app outages at JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo. The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.12% and Brent crude about $92.

## Datadog (DDOG): the story behind the slide

**In short:** the drop is real news layered on a market-wide sell-off, not a collapse in the business. Datadog's (cloud monitoring and security software) biggest customer, widely reported to be OpenAI, has cut how much it uses Datadog. Management then guided the fourth quarter at about the same revenue as the third. Before that, the stock had already been caught in October's "AI will eat software" sell-off. Today's 6.1% drop had no news about Datadog itself. It came with a broad tech and AI rout the day before Nvidia reports.

### How the price got here (daily closes, stockanalysis.com)
- **Oct 12:** 52-week high of 300.68 during the session, close 287.29. The stock had climbed from a 52-week low near 98.
- **Oct 14–16:** fell to 247 in the first software sell-off, then recovered to about 280 by Oct 26–28.
- **Oct 29–30:** dropped to 265.84 and then 235.27 (down 11.5%). ServiceNow fell 27% on fears that AI will cut demand for software, and weak Amazon and Intel results followed. There was no Datadog-specific news.
- **Nov 2:** 216.10. **Nov 3:** 220.52.
- **Nov 4, earnings day (reported before the open):** gapped open at 199.74 and closed at 188.72, down 14.4%, on 13.2M shares.
- **Nov 5:** 174.60, down 7.5%, with a low of 170.50. That low is the screen's 20-day low.
- **Nov 6–13:** traded sideways between about 173 and 189. Closes ran 179.04, 179.62, 178.40, 184.38, 184.46 and 184.16. Nov 13 opened at 188 and faded, a sign sellers were still there.
- **Nov 16:** opened at 182.41, which was also the day's high. It fell all session to close at 172.86, just above the low of 172.39, on 3.35M shares. The after-hours price was 172.50. It closed weak, and the 170.50 floor is about 1.4% below.

### The fundamentals (Q3 report, Nov 4, SEC 8-K)
- **Q3 revenue:** $1.197B, up 35%. That was about $52M above the top of guidance.
- **Profit:** adjusted EPS of $0.81 against $0.64 expected. Adjusted operating margin was 28%, up from 23%. Free cash flow was $251M.
- **Forward-looking measures:**
  - Billings were $1.16B, up 30%.
  - Remaining performance obligations (contracted revenue not yet booked) were $3.85B, up 38%, and the part due within a year grew in the mid-30s%.
  - Net revenue retention was in the low 120s%.
  - About 4,860 customers spend over $100k a year, up 20%.
  - Infrastructure Monitoring passed $2B in annual recurring revenue.
- **Q4 guidance:** revenue of $1.19–1.20B, which is flat with Q3 and 25–26% growth on a year ago. Adjusted EPS guidance is $0.69–0.71.
- **Full-year 2026 guidance:** raised to $4.515–4.525B (about 32% growth), with adjusted EPS of $2.73–2.75.
- **The largest customer:**
  - The cut was first flagged in August. The stock fell about 17% that day, then won back about half of it within days.
  - Q3 usage fell but stayed above the contracted minimum. Q4 guidance assumes the customer pays only that minimum.
  - Bernstein and others put the cut at about $100M of yearly revenue. Datadog has not named the customer.
- **Excluding that customer:** management says Q4 growth works out to the low-to-mid 30s%. Growth from non-AI customers has sped up for five quarters in a row, to the high 20s%.
- **Other AI customers:** some are renewing early at lower prices in exchange for larger commitments, which is a short-term headwind. Management also warned that Q4 usage can dip from late-December holidays and code freezes.
- **Conservative guidance:** management guides low, and it beat the Q3 top by about $52M. A similar beat would put Q4 revenue near $1.24–1.25B.

### Sentiment and positioning
- **Analysts:** no rating downgrades. Most cut price targets on Nov 5:
  - Citi: 290
  - Wells Fargo: 300
  - Rosenblatt: 285
  - Barclays: 262
  - DA Davidson: 275
  - RBC: 270
  - BTIG: 260

  The MarketBeat consensus is about $275–278. Even so, the price has fallen almost every day since.
- **Insiders:** 467 sales and no purchases over six months (Quiver, AI-generated summary). The CEO sold about $191M and the CTO about $151M, mostly through scheduled sales, but it weighs on sentiment.
- **Technical sellers:** Cestrian Capital moved to a "Stop" rating after the stock broke its 200-day average (about 200) and its $195 stop level.

### Valuation (rough, my arithmetic)
- At 172.86 with about 379M diluted shares, the market value is about $65B. Net of $5.2B cash, the enterprise value is about $60B.
- That is about 63x this year's adjusted EPS guidance and about 12–13x annualized revenue.
- In August, at about 260, it traded near 18x forward revenue. The stock is much cheaper than its own history but still not cheap in absolute terms.

### Market backdrop today (Nov 16)
- The Nasdaq fell about 2.5% and the S&P 500 about 1.9%, its biggest three-day drop since June. Chip stocks fell 5.3%.
- The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.15%, which hurts expensive growth stocks.
- Reports also cite turmoil around Nvidia's leadership (Jensen Huang reportedly resigned as CEO on Nov 12) and new limits on AI chip exports.
- Datadog's fall on light volume fits a market-wide de-risking more than a new problem at the company.

### Events in the 1–10 session window
1. **Nvidia earnings, Tue Nov 17, after the close (around 3:00 PM CT or later).** This is the main swing factor for AI-linked stocks. A relief rally would probably lift Datadog's oversold bounce, while a bad reaction could break 170.50.
2. **Anthropic's IPO, priced Wed Nov 18 in the evening and trading Thu Nov 19.** Anthropic is plausibly one of Datadog's large AI customers, though that is not confirmed. A strong debut could lift AI-infrastructure sentiment, but new AI stock supply could also pull money away from names like Datadog.
3. **No Datadog-specific catalyst** until Q4 earnings in mid-February. The risk is another AI customer cutting back.

### How I read it for a 1–10 session trade
**For a bounce:**
- The stock is deeply oversold: RSI 28, 3.5 average daily ranges below its 20-day average, and down about 43% from the October high.
- The business is not broken. It beat Q3, raised the full year, contracted revenue is up 38%, and growth excluding the big customer is in the low-to-mid 30s%.
- Guidance is set to be beaten, and analyst targets are 50% or more above the price.
- Today's fall had no Datadog-specific news and came on below-average volume.

**Against a bounce:**
- The stock has not turned. It closed at the day's low, the Nov 13 fade shows sellers using rallies, and it is right at the post-earnings floor of 170.50.
- Q4 guidance is flat quarter on quarter, which removes the "growth stock" reason to own it until February.
- Concentration in AI customers and lower-priced renewals is an open-ended risk.
- Insiders sell steadily, and technical traders and stop rules are already out below the 200-day average.
- The whole market turns on Nvidia tomorrow.

**My conclusion:** this is a stock that fell with a news story and the whole market, sitting on support. It is a candidate only if it holds 170.50 and the Nvidia reaction is benign. A clean break below 170.50 on volume would mean the post-earnings base failed, with no obvious support until the August-era lows.

- The web-search budget ran out partway through. I could not check what drove the rally from 98 to 300 earlier in 2026, insider filings directly, or any report of OpenAI building its own monitoring tools.

## The story in brief

ServiceNow had the **worst single-day drop in its history** after its third-quarter results, released after the close on Oct 28. The quarter itself was fine. The guidance for future contract growth was the problem, and it came on top of a year in which investors already feared AI would eat into software sales. Since that crash the stock has gone sideways around $100 for about a week, holding between roughly $97 and $104 rather than falling further. The fear about AI hurting software keeps getting refreshed by news (an Anthropic product launch on Nov 10, and an Anthropic stock-market listing this week), while management keeps arguing against it.

## What happened, step by step

**1. The Oct 28 quarterly report.** Revenue was $4.106B, up 20.5% and above the $4.09B expected. Subscription revenue was $3,988M, up 21%. Contracted revenue due in the next 12 months ("cRPO") was $13.65B, up 21% in constant currency, which beat guidance by about 1 percentage point. Adjusted EPS was $1.00 against $1.02 expected, the first miss in six quarters. Management blamed acquisition costs.
- **What sank it:** guidance that contracted revenue would grow only **18.5%** next quarter, against about 19.8% expected.
- **Management's explanation:**
  - Some renewals closed early, in Q3 instead of Q4.
  - More customers bought the on-premises version.
  - Some Armis contracts can be cancelled by the customer, so they are left out of cRPO.
  - Extra help on large AI deals is booked as services revenue, about a 0.5 point drag on Q4 subscription growth.
- **The underlying issue: growth without acquisitions is slower.**
  - The company has spent $9.2B on acquisitions this year (Armis, Veza, Moveworks), and goodwill went from $3.6B to $10.0B.
  - Guggenheim estimates growth without those deals at about **17–18%**. Morgan Stanley puts the comparable contract growth at about 18%, down from 19%.
  - KeyBanc (rated sell, $110 target) argues teens growth can't support a premium price.
  - The bull case is that these accounting effects are temporary. Evercore sees about a 1 point drag on 2027 subscription growth from them.
- **Positives in the report:**
  - The 2026 target for new AI contract value was raised to $1.7B, from $1.5B and originally $1B.
  - AI contract value grew 65%.
  - The full-year free cash flow margin target was raised to 36%.
  - The full-year subscription forecast was raised.
  - Customers renewed at a 98% rate.
- **Weaker points:**
  - GAAP operating margin fell to 9.5% from 17%.
  - Interest expense was $81M versus $6M a year ago, because of new debt.
  - **No share buybacks in Q3** (versus $584M a year earlier).
- **The move:** the stock was $154.60 when results came out and about $105 a day later. Sources disagree on the exact one-day drop (19%, "over 20%" and 27% are all quoted).

**2. Analysts mostly cut targets but kept buy ratings.**
- Morgan Stanley: $180 to $160.
- Wells Fargo: $190 to $175.
- Citi: $170 to $157.
- Mizuho: $165. TD Cowen: $160. RBC: $165. Barclays: $152. Baird: $185.
- Cantor raised its target to $201 on Oct 26, before the report.
- KeyBanc: sell, $110.
- The average target is about $154.50. Almost every target is far above the current $99.

**3. Since then.**
- Nov 4–5: a third round of layoffs this year. CEO McDermott called a smaller workforce "a gorgeous situation" and told investors to "relax" about AI.
- **Nov 10: down 3.1–5% to $99.61**, while the software sector fell only about 1.3%. Benzinga tied it to Anthropic launching Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Data, which revived fears for software sellers. I could not open that article or confirm those product names. Another outlet cited a planned insider sale filing.
- Nov 11: up 3.3%.
- Nov 12: down 2.1% on low volume. A law firm (Pomerantz) is soliciting investors for a possible claim, with no finding of wrongdoing.
- Nov 12–13: at a BMO conference, management said **over half of quarterly revenue isn't priced per user**, and that it expects user counts to keep growing through 2027. It also launched an "Autonomous CRM Engine," available to selected customers only. Kyndryl expanded its partnership.
- Nov 13: up 1.9%.
- **Nov 16: down 2.9% to about $99.32 on about 10.7M shares, half the normal 21M.** There was no company news. The whole market fell: Nasdaq down 2.5% (its third straight loss), S&P 500 down 1.9%, VIX (the market's fear gauge) briefly at 24, led by chip stocks ahead of Nvidia's results. NOW roughly kept pace with the Nasdaq, so this looks like a market-wide drop, not company-specific selling.

**4. The bigger picture.** NOW is down about 29–33% this year and about 40% over 12 months. Software has sold off in waves this year whenever Anthropic released something: the Claude Cowork plugins in February, Mythos in April, and now November. The April low probably matches the 52-week low of $81.24, but I could not confirm the date. The stock now trades at about 21 times next year's expected earnings, versus a 73 times trailing figure that is distorted by acquisition charges.

## What could move it in the next 1–10 sessions

Bloomberg's Nov 16 headline also says the listing is "on horizon," but I could not open that article. A hot debut of the company most tied to "AI replaces software" could push the fear about NOW further. It could also pull money out of software to pay for the new shares.

The next two sessions bring two big tests of the AI-versus-software story at once (Nvidia, then the Anthropic listing). Each Anthropic event this year has hit NOW harder than its peers. Behind the 20-day underperformance against XLF (the financials ETF) are three slower themes: the Democratic sweep of Congress on Nov 3, a Fed that has started raising rates again with the 10-year yield above 5%, and doubts about how much banks have lent to private credit and other non-bank lenders. **Note:** I used up the web-search limit for this turn before finishing. I could not confirm a few things: why the basket fell behind XLF over 20 days specifically, how the market reacted to the election results bank by bank, and third-quarter details for PNC, USB, TFC and Citi. ### 1. What happened today
- **The outage.** Chase had a "technical issue" that slowed some transactions. Downdetector logged about 3,300 to 4,700 complaints for Chase, about 2,000 for BofA and over 1,000 for Wells Fargo. Complaints also spiked at US Bank, Citi, Capital One and others.
  - JPM blamed a software bug in its own on-premise hardware systems. It said there was no sign of a cyberattack and that customers kept access to their funds.
  - JPM said it was fixed Monday evening and called it "not a systemic issue." Other banks were only hit when a payment involved JPM, for example Zelle payments at US Bank.
  - BofA, PNC, Capital One and Truist said their own systems were not disrupted. Wells Fargo and Citi did not comment.
  - It followed a Microsoft Outlook and Teams disruption and an FAA communications failure in the days before. Officials said these were unrelated, but together they made "concentrated tech risk" a talking point.
- **Stock moves.** JPM, BAC, WFC and C each fell about 2% to 2.5%, and the KBW bank index lost 1.6%.
  - That fits your screen: JPM was worst at -2.3% and TFC best at -0.8%. The regional banks were not affected by the outage, so they held up.
  - JPM is now around $338, just below its 50-day average of about $340.5 and well above its 200-day average of about $325.
- **The wider market.** The S&P 500 fell about 1.9%, the Dow 1.4% and the Nasdaq about 2.5%.
  - Nvidia fell about 4% ahead of its earnings on Tuesday, and new US limits on chip access abroad hit chip stocks.
  - The Anthropic IPO, expected to start trading Thursday Nov 19 at about $1.4T, may be pulling money out of other AI stocks.
  - **My view:** Most of today's gap against XLF looks like a JPM event (a headline, already fixed) on top of a broad high-beta sell-off. JPM is a large weight inside XLF too, so XLF took part of the same hit.

### 2. The slower story behind the 20-day underperformance
- **Rates and the Fed.**
  - The Fed raised rates on Sep 16, its first hike in more than three years, to 3.75% to 4.00%. TFC and USB each fell about 4% that day.
  - October inflation came in hot: consumer prices were higher than expected, and producer prices rose 6.5% year over year, the highest in almost four years.
  - Traders now treat a December hike as close to certain, and Deutsche Bank expects three in a row. The 10-year yield was 5.13% today, after 5.17% on Friday. The 2-year was 4.83%, so the gap between them is about 30 basis points.

Capital-rule changes expected in December could free about $18B across JPM, BAC, C and others. That relief comes from the Basel and GSIB surcharge re-proposals, which apply only to the eight largest banks, so it would help JPM, BAC, C and WFC, not PNC, USB or TFC.
- **Private credit.**
  - The Fed says bank lending to non-bank financial firms passed $2.8T in the second quarter, and it flagged data-centre and AI financing links. A Forbes piece from today puts the eight largest banks' exposure at $1.77T, about 169% of their core capital if undrawn credit lines are counted.

**1. Since the Iran war, these stocks move opposite to oil.** Paint and coatings makers buy solvents and resins made from oil. They raise their own prices only months after their costs rise. Bank of America found that before the Strait of Hormuz disruption, oil explained less than 1% of SHW's daily moves; after it, about 39%, with the stocks falling as oil rose. It saw the same in PPG and ECL. It also found coatings makers pass on 90% or more of cost increases within about three months.

- **SHW:** gross margin fell to 47.8% from 49.2%, and earnings per share missed slightly.
- **PPG:** its Industrial segment margin fell 260 basis points (2.6 points) on cost inflation.
- **ECL:** it added an energy surcharge.

- Brent fell about 16% in the week of Nov 2 to 6. That was its worst week since Covid, on reports of a Qatar-brokered Iranian offer to reopen Hormuz.

Management still guided low to mid single-digit raw material inflation for 2027, heaviest in the first half, and a muted, choppy demand outlook.
- **PPG** raised the midpoint of its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.90 to $8.10. One caveat: its Industrial customers' prices follow raw-material indexes, so falling costs pass back to them with a lag.

## AXON: what happened

**Short version:** a high-multiple growth stock lost its "can't miss" status. The first damage came over the summer and fall, from new borrowing and weaker cash generation. Then the Q3 report (8-K dated Thursday, Nov 5) did three things at once: it cut 2026 revenue guidance, cut free cash flow guidance, and committed another $1.2B to Skydio. The stock went from 424.18 on Nov 4 to 306.44 today, down about 28%. Since then it has traded sideways between roughly 291 and 321 for seven sessions and has not bounced.

### Before the report
- **From the high:** Trefis puts the fall at -49.9% from Aug 14 to Nov 12 (the S&P 500 lost 2.2% over the same window) and about -44.5% year to date. Motorola Solutions, the closest peer, rose about 14% over that stretch, so this is about Axon, not the sector. One Motley Fool piece says the stock is about 64% below its all-time high.
- **Sept 15, -9.8%:** Axon announced $1.0B of convertible-note borrowing. In total it issued $1.15B of notes in the quarter, partly to pay for Skydio.
- **October:** the stock chopped between about 377 and 438 on light volume of 0.6 to 1.5M shares a day.
- **Nov 5, -9.8% during regular hours:** high 434, low 368, close 382.56, on 3.6M shares. That is unusual if the report came after the close. One source says the shares fell as much as 18% before the open. **I could not confirm the timing or the cause of the Nov 5 regular-session drop.**

### The Q3 report (from the 8-K)
- **Misses:** revenue was $908.6M (+28%) against about $935M expected. Adjusted EPS was $1.72 against about $1.89. Adjusted EBITDA of $235.7M actually beat.
- **Guidance cut:** full-year 2026 revenue growth went from 32–34% to about 30% ($3.61–3.63B). Q4 revenue guidance is $990M–$1.01B against about $1.07B expected, the slowest growth since late 2021.
- **Cause of the cut:** three federal Dedrone deployments worth about $130M slipped out of 2026. Dedrone is Axon's counter-drone business. About $30M was due in Q3 and $100M in Q4. Management says this is timing, not lost demand, and that it will guide more conservatively from now on.
- **Cash, the bigger bear point:**
  - Q3 free cash flow was -$18.9M.
  - Full-year free cash flow guidance fell from $450M to $350–400M, which needs about $450M in Q4 alone to hit the midpoint.
  - Inventory is up 69% since December, to $579M.
  - Net debt is $1.2B ($2.9B of notes against $1.7B of cash). It rises further once the cash part of the Skydio payment goes out.
- **Margins:** adjusted gross margin fell from 62.7% to 59.2%. Connected-devices adjusted gross margin fell from 52.1% to 44.6%. The causes were lower-margin counter-drone sales, higher memory-chip costs, and the absence of last year's tariff refunds. TASER revenue fell about 2%.
- **Skydio:** $1.2B (about 60% cash, 40% stock) takes Axon's stake to 37% and makes it Skydio's exclusive public-safety distributor in the US and Canada. That puts it more directly against Motorola. The market read it as balance-sheet risk.
- **What held up:**
  - Software and services revenue +43% (accelerating from 36% in Q2).
  - Annual recurring revenue $1.75B (+40%).
  - Net revenue retention 126%.
  - Future contracted bookings $15.8B (+39%).
  - AI recurring revenue above $100M.
  - Large state corrections wins of $258M and $115M.

### Since the report
- **Nov 6, -18.2%:** close 313.00 on 5.2M shares.
- **Nov 9–10:** the low came on Nov 10 at 291.45.
- **Nov 11–13:** a recovery attempt to 315.43 on falling volume.
- **Today:** the stock opened at 313.71, reached 318.45, and closed at 306.44, near the day's low at 304. It was turned back at the top of the range again.
- **Volume** has faded from 5.2M to 1.3–1.6M shares a day. That is still about twice the October pace, so "normal" on our screen is measured against a 20-day average that includes the report.
- **Analysts** cut targets but mostly kept their ratings:
  - Raymond James: $675 to $475, Outperform.
  - Needham: $750 to $500, Buy.
  - Piper Sandler: $561 to $540, Overweight.
  - Barclays: $507, Overweight.
  - RBC, TD Cowen and Baird also lowered targets.
  - Craig-Hallum downgraded to Neutral.
- **Law-firm "investigation" notices** have appeared. These usually follow a big drop and I'd treat them as noise.
- **Valuation:** about 7x sales and about 96x trailing reported earnings, with a market value near $33B. On consensus next-year EPS of about $9.74, that is roughly 31x.

### What this means for the next 1 to 10 sessions
- **No scheduled company catalyst:** Q4 results are expected in February 2027.
- **Tax-loss selling:** a stock down about 45% this year is an obvious candidate for December selling, which can cap rebounds.
- **Things that could move it:**
  - The Skydio deal closing.
  - News that a Dedrone federal deployment has landed.
  - More target cuts or a downgrade.
- **Trade framing:** the 291–321 range has held for seven sessions. A daily close below about 291 would mean the post-report low has failed. A close above about 321 would be the first sign the stock has turned. Today's rejection near the top of the range argues there is no turn yet.
- **Bull case:** the shortfall is timing, software is accelerating, and the stock sits at a two-year low.
- **Bear case:** reported growth now leans on lumpy, low-margin federal hardware, cash is weakening while debt rises, and the sellers are big institutions resetting a premium multiple. Repricings like that rarely finish in two weeks.

I ran out of web searches (the session cap) before I could do separate searches on the bull case, why value stocks are winning, and the September Fed hike. Those parts below come from articles I had already read, not their own sources.

## Where prices are
- **Monday's close:** the S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59, the Nasdaq fell 2.49% to 24,510 and the Dow fell 1.41% to 51,608. It was the third straight down day. The S&P hit a record above 7,800 on Oct. 6, so it is now about 5% below that.

- **Fear gauges:** the VIX (the market's volatility index) closed at 23.4. The semiconductor index fell 5.3%.
- **Rates:** the 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.13% and the 2-year about 4.83%. The dollar had its highest close since April 2025.
- **Commodities and crypto:** WTI oil is about $86, gold about $3,860, copper below $6, silver about $47.50 and bitcoin about $64–65k.
- **The level everyone is watching:** the Nov. 5 low of 7,353.73 on the S&P. Monday closed 0.9% above it, and a close below it is widely framed as turning a retest into a breakdown.
- **Overnight:** futures are flat to +0.2% as of about 7:45 PM CT. Nvidia fell further after hours, and Asia is opening 1–1.5% lower.

## The arguments driving prices

**1. Is the AI build-out about to slow? (the main story)**
- **The midterms started it.** Democrats swept the House and Senate on Nov. 3, and candidates and ballot measures against new data centers did well. On Nov. 5 the Nasdaq fell about 5%, its worst day since April 2025, and the chip index had its worst day since March 2020.
- **What the bears say:**
  - Sanders is calling for a national data center moratorium.
  - Texas's governor-elect has proposed a statewide freeze on new permits.
  - Meta's president said building in the US is "going to be harder."
  - Dan Ives now sees tech capital spending growth peaking in 2027, not 2028–29, and expects 10–20% of planned US data centers to be dropped or delayed.
- **What the bulls say:** most of the capacity due in 2027 is already being built, a national moratorium would be vetoed, and the real drag only starts around 2028.
- **Where it hurts most:** AI hardware. On Monday Sandisk fell 8.6%, Micron 7.6%, and Intel, Dell, Marvell, Vertiv, Corning, Ciena and Coherent each fell 7–8.5%.

**2. Nvidia without Jensen Huang, plus tighter chip export rules**
- **What happened:**
  - Huang admitted an affair after reports that one partner was a Chinese spy. He resigned on Nov. 12.
  - CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey Jones is the first board chair.
  - Congress is threatening to subpoena Huang.
  - A petition to bring him back has about 180k signatures, and Musk backs it. Trump said he "would not mind" a return. CNBC says the board is not considering it, and Treasury Secretary Bessent reportedly wants an outside CEO.
- **The stock:** down about 24% in November, on pace for its worst month since April 2022. It has lost over $2T in value from its October peak and is now the third-largest US company. Mizuho calls the gap versus the chip index (-32% vs -23%) the lost "founder premium."
- **The export rule (issued Monday):**
  - Data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil now need a license to receive advanced Nvidia and AMD chips.
  - Data centers anywhere need a license to give China-based companies remote access to these chips.
  - AMD fell 5.6% on Monday.
  - The administration is divided on this, Congress has four bills that would add more controls, and Singapore has pushed back.
- **Earnings, Tuesday about 3:20 PM CT:**
  - Consensus is about $109B revenue and $2.47 EPS.
  - Options imply a move of about 8%, roughly $341B in market value.
  - The open questions are whether the 70% growth forecast for fiscal 2028 holds, what export exposure looks like, buybacks, its financing of other AI companies, and whether the product roadmap changes.

**3. Will the Anthropic IPO lift the AI trade or drain money from it?**
- **Terms:** prices Wednesday night and starts trading Thursday on Nasdaq as ANT. The range is $70–78, raising up to about $64B. Seven tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft, are buying another $26B privately at the IPO price. Valuation is about $1.3–1.4T fully diluted.
- **Demand:** reported as about 6–7x oversubscribed.
- **The warning signs:**
  - The valuation is down from hopes of about $2T in September.
  - This year's 10 biggest IPOs are on average about 20% below their offer prices.
  - Vanda expects record retail demand, about $250M on day one, and warns that money could come out of other AI stocks.
- **How people are positioning:** bullish options bets on Microsoft are at their lowest since 2022. Call buying is up in Amazon and Alphabet, which each own more than 5% of Anthropic.
- **Other effects:** BofA says the deal is pushing smaller IPOs, biotech included, into 2027.
- **A side argument about governance:** Anthropic has five share classes and SpaceX two. Fortune argues Nvidia's board removing Huang is the exception, not a new standard.

**4. A Fed that is raising rates, with the 10-year above 5%**
- **The setup:** the Fed hiked on Sept. 16 and held in October. BofA now calls that hold "increasingly a mistake." Fed funds are 3.75–4.00%.
- **Inflation data:**
  - October CPI rose 0.4% (0.3% expected). Core rose 0.3% (0.2% expected), with core services speeding up again.
  - October payrolls rose 165k against 65k expected.
- **Pricing:** a 25bp hike on Dec. 9 is about 91% priced and a 50bp hike about 9%. Waller said 50bp "should be considered." Markets price about 83bp of hikes through November 2027.
- **Debt worry:** Fed Governor Bowman struck a hawkish tone on corporate debt. That matters for hyperscalers that borrow to build AI capacity: Goldman expects $296B of hyperscaler debt issuance in 2026 and $440B in 2027, with large off-balance-sheet obligations on top.
- **Mixed data:** the Empire State factory index came in at 7.8 against 16.7 expected, so not all data is hot.
- **Why tech is hit hardest:** a 10-year above 5% lowers what long-dated growth earnings are worth.

**5. The rotation into value stocks**
- The Russell 1000 Value is up about 25% this year while Growth is down about 1.8%. That would be value's best year relative to growth since 2000.
- Low-volatility stocks beat high-beta stocks by the widest margin in over three years through October.
- **Winning:** staples (Coca-Cola at a record, Tyson +8.7%), managed care (Centene +4.9%, Elevance +3.9%), utilities and real estate.
- **The open question:** is this healthy broadening, with Q3 S&P earnings growth about 31% and spreading beyond the megacaps, or just rotating the same money around? Retail investors have piled into defensives, which some say now look overbought.

**6. Other stories in the background**
- **Oil and the Iran war:**
  - The Strait of Hormuz is still disrupted. October had the most ships attacked of any month in the war, and a third US carrier has arrived.
  - Even so, the IEA sees a supply surplus of about 2M barrels a day, and crude futures fell almost 25% in a month. Energy is no longer a source of inflation fear.
  - Congress, now divided, must fund the war before the Dec. 11 deadline, so a government shutdown is possible.
- **Crypto:**

  - Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy are down 6–8%.
- **Metals and the dollar:**

I couldn't find one clear reason for CVI to bounce in the next 1-10 sessions. The 30% drop is mostly a known, priced event. The likely next drivers are crude and refining margins, which were falling today, and a lot of newly sold stock is overhanging the price.

**What happened**

- **Before the deal.** CVI ran from about $20 to a $63.51 high on October 14. It was a small refiner earning record margins: refining supply was disrupted by the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz, and damaged Russian refineries cut fuel supply. A $70 crack spread (what refiners earn per barrel) in July, against a normal $15-25, made it look like a "supercycle". It closed at $55.92 on November 2.
- **November 3, the trigger.** On the same day CVR:
  - Reported a record Q3: adjusted EPS of $4.00 against about $2.91 expected, revenue of $3.28B (up 69%), EBITDA of $582M and $593M of free cash flow.
  - Agreed to buy Marathon's St. Paul Park (Minnesota) and Mandan (North Dakota) refineries plus about 590 fuel stations for about $4.2B. That takes capacity from about 207,000 to about 384,000 barrels a day.
  - Launched a $750M stock sale: $500M of new shares, and $250M from Icahn's holding company, which controls about 71%. The final pricing release covers only 10.5M company shares at $47.55, net about $490M, and says no Icahn shares are included. So Icahn's sale appears to have been dropped at pricing. I couldn't confirm why.
- **How the deal is paid for.** A $2.5B secured bridge loan (a lender meeting for a term loan is planned), a $500M equity commitment from Icahn's company, an $800M equity investment from Trafigura (a large commodity trader), and cash.
  - Pro forma debt is about $3.8B, under 2x 2026 pro forma EBITDA. Management had been aiming for about $1B of gross debt.
  - Close is targeted for year-end, pending antitrust clearance.
  - I couldn't find the price or terms of the Icahn or Trafigura equity. If they come in as common stock near today's price, that is roughly another 30M+ shares on top of about 111M.
- **Why it sold off.** Buyers worried about debt, dilution, and buying refineries near a margin peak. Q3 also flattered: GAAP EPS of $5.67 includes a one-time $253M EPA waiver (exemption from a renewable-fuel obligation) for its Wynnewood refinery.

**How the price traded**

| Date | Close | Volume |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 2 | 55.92 | 0.77M |
| Nov 3 | 48.60 | 3.25M |
| Nov 4 (deal priced at $47.55) | 43.01 | 13.4M |

- **Buyers in the share sale are underwater.** It broke below the $47.55 offer price on day one, on very heavy volume, and now sits about 18% under it. The underwriters' extra-share option is out of the money, so any support from them has likely ended.
- **It has based for 8 sessions.** Since November 5 it has held a narrow $38-41 range on falling volume. The 20-day low of $37.22 sits at the bottom of that range.
- **The screen's volume reading understates today.** "0.8x normal" is measured against an average inflated by the offering days. Today's 1.8M shares is still more than double the pre-deal normal of about 0.7M.
- **Today's drop was mostly the sector, not news.**
  - Brent fell 2.6% to $93.34 and WTI 2.4% to $86.41, on recovering flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
  - Marathon and Valero each fell about 2.7-3%.
  - CVI also went ex-dividend today: $0.10 against $39 (record date November 16, payable November 23).
  - The only company news was Mizuho upgrading it to Neutral from Underperform, with the target cut to $47 from $52.

**Bull case**

- **Cheap if margins hold.** At $39 it is worth about $4.35B. Pro forma EBITDA for the first nine months of 2026 is about $2.0B. The deal price was under 3.5x 2026 EBITDA, and management says the assets earn about $800M in a normal year. They expect more than 50% EPS and free-cash-flow accretion and about $70M of synergies.
- **Management expects strong margins to last.** They see above-normal margins for 12-24 months, through 2027. Q4 throughput guidance of 210,000-225,000 barrels a day is above the prior quarter's guide.
- **The fall is out of line with peers.** Mizuho says CVI is down about 36% in a month against about 17% for peers. The stock is still up about 62% this year, so the gap could close.
- **Analysts are moving off Sell.** Mizuho's upgrade is the first move off Sell. The consensus target is about $46.

**Bear case**

- **Margins are fading.** The EIA expected crack spreads to "narrow meaningfully in Q4 2026." Hormuz flows are recovering, refiners had their worst day since April 2025 in October, and Valero was downgraded to Sell on October 26. That is the opposite of what a newly levered buyer needs.
- **Supply overhang.** About 10.5M new shares sit underwater, with more equity from Icahn and Trafigura still to come at unknown terms. The term-loan syndication and deal close by year-end are near-term events.
- **The regulatory waiver can come back as a headline.** CVR leans on EPA small-refinery waivers, and the Mandan deal valuation assumes no future waivers.
- **Analysts lean bearish.** The consensus is Sell or Reduce. Goldman is at Sell with a $50 target, set before the deal.

There is no scheduled company event in the window that I found, apart from possible deal-financing or antitrust news. The stock trades with crude and the refiner group, which fell today. The setup is a post-offering base at $38-41 with the 20-day low at $37.22 just below. Breaking that low would mean the base failed. A stabilizing refiner group and a recovery toward $41 would point to the gap with peers closing.

## Assurant (AIZ): research for the 10:45 PM CT, Mon 2026-11-16 journal

**Bottom line:** the run is backed by real news. The Nov 3 quarterly report was a big beat, and the rise has been an orderly two-week climb with no new information since about Nov 10. In the last week the stock has gone mostly sideways in a band of about 318 to 327, just under its 52-week high. A gap-and-run from here would need a new catalyst; a sharp break would need the market's rotation to reverse. One likely catalyst is due inside the 1-10 session window: the yearly dividend increase.

### The story
1. **The quarter (reported Nov 3, after the close):** adjusted EPS was $6.15, or $6.46 without storm losses, against a consensus of about $4.65-4.75. That is roughly a 35-39% beat. Revenue was $3.53B, up 9% and a little above the $3.47-3.48B estimate. Without storm losses, adjusted EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax and write-offs) and adjusted EPS both rose 12%. The CEO called it "positioning us for a record year."
   - **Global Lifestyle:** EBITDA up 15%. Inside it, Connected Living (phone protection, trade-ins and device logistics) earnings rose 23%, helped by new programs with US Cellular, Best Buy and Chase. Assurant now covers 69M devices, and devices it serviced rose by 2.8M from a year ago to 7.6M. The auto business was up 9% underlying, and its written premiums rose 25%, partly from timing.
   - **Global Housing:** EBITDA without storms up 11%, on fewer claims and cheaper reinsurance. The Freedom Mortgage contract added about 2.6M loans and is still ramping up.
2. **Guidance raised:** for 2026, EBITDA up about 10% and EPS up by a low double-digit rate, both without storm losses. Excluding the drop in reserve releases, EPS growth would be mid-teens. Buybacks were raised to $350M, the top of the range, and $469M was left under the authorization at Oct 31.
3. **Analysts raised their targets after the report:**
   - Keefe, Bruyette & Woods: $345 (Nov 5)
   - Piper Sandler: $356 (Nov 9)
   - UBS: $331 to $377 (Nov 10)
   - Morgan Stanley: $330 to $360, Overweight. MarketBeat dates it today, Nov 16; GuruFocus dates it Nov 10.
   - The consensus target is about $346, about 7% above today's close. Ratings are 8 Buy or Strong Buy.
4. **Small acquisition:** Assurant bought Protection Point (Nov 5), a Canadian administrator of equipment protection plans. It was already an exclusive partner; terms were not disclosed. It does not move the stock.
5. **Path of the price:** about 296 before earnings, then 302 pre-market on Nov 4, about 309 on Nov 5, 322.48 on Nov 10 (on normal volume), a 52-week high of about 326-327, and 323.80 today. So the 15% gain over twenty sessions came mostly between Nov 3 and Nov 10. Since then the stock has drifted sideways.

### Why it rose on a day SPY fell 1.9%
- **The market:** the selloff was driven by AI and chip stocks around Nvidia. The Nasdaq fell 2.5%, the VIX (the market's fear gauge) jumped 19% to 22.9, and only 145 S&P 500 members rose. Only consumer staples and utilities finished up.
- **AIZ's profile:** it has a low beta of 0.52 (it moves about half as much as the market) and its earnings have nothing to do with AI. That makes it a natural place for money leaving tech.
- **No news of its own:** none of the market wrap-ups mention AIZ. Today's move is best read as relative strength from being defensive plus the Morgan Stanley note. Financials as a group fell 0.85%, so AIZ is beating its own sector.

### Catalysts inside 1-10 sessions
- **Dividend raise and buyback (likely):** Assurant announced its last two raises on Nov 19, 2024 and Nov 13, 2025, the second with a new $700M buyback. I found no 2026 announcement yet. A 22nd straight yearly raise is likely soon, but this is a pattern, not a confirmed date. It is a mild positive and usually not a big mover.
- **Market calendar this week:**
  - Tue Nov 17: retail sales and Home Depot before the open; Nvidia earnings after the close.
  - Wed Nov 18: the Anthropic IPO prices; trading starts Thu Nov 19.
  - Futures put about a 91% chance on a 25bp Fed rate *hike* in December. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.12%.
  - If AI stocks bounce after Nvidia, money could rotate back out of defensives. That is the main risk to the reason AIZ is up right now.
- **No earnings until about early February**, when 2027 guidance is also due.

### Risks and soft spots
- **Hurricane Isaias:** it hit Destin, Florida on Oct 9 as a Category 2, the first US hurricane landfall since 2024. Estimates of total insured losses run $1-4.5B. Assurant's lender-placed home insurance has Florida exposure, so the fourth quarter will carry storm losses. Guidance leaves storms out, though, and I found no estimate from Assurant itself.
- **Other soft spots:** reserve releases are smaller than last year (a $52M drag on 2026), part of the auto growth was timing, the business depends on a few big partners, and phone-protection pricing is competitive.
- **Insider selling:** I found no November 2026 Form 4 filings. The 2025 sales were under pre-set 10b5-1 plans.
- **Valuation:** about 15x trailing earnings and about 13.5x the 2026 EPS estimate of $23.93. That is not stretched for a company growing earnings at a low double-digit rate.

### How to read it
The fundamentals behind the run are strong and new, and every revision since the report has gone up. The price is the problem. The stock is stretched (RSI 78, 3.4 average daily ranges above its 20-day average) and has already gone sideways for about a week under 326-327. That looks like the post-earnings drift digesting rather than ending.
- **Upside case:** a clean close above about 327 on a dividend or buyback release, or on more defensive buying if Nvidia disappoints.
- **Downside case:** if the AI trade bounces on Wednesday, money rotates out of defensives and the stock likely slides back toward about 310-315, where it was trading around Nov 5-9.
- **Shorting it:** nothing in the story argues for a short.
